content:
Apple has filed its proposal regarding the commission it would charge for transactions conducted outside the App Store system in the Epic Games case. Here are the details.

Apple Files Proposal for App Store External Transaction Commission

After multiple attempts to stay the district court proceedings—which will determine how much (or even whether) Apple can charge for transactions conducted outside the App Store's in-app purchase (IAP) system—Apple has finally filed its proposal, setting out the proposed fee structure.

Just as Apple filed its proposal, the Supreme Court rejected the company's request to stay the lower court proceedings. Apple is awaiting the Supreme Court's review of whether it is in contempt of court for charging a 27% commission on transactions outside the App Store, after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative purchase methods.

Apple argued before both the lower court and the Supreme Court that the Supreme Court's ruling could affect the outcome of the fee determination proceedings, and therefore those proceedings should be stayed until the Supreme Court issues its ruling. However, the Supreme Court rejected Apple's request, allowing the lower court proceedings to continue while review is underway.

Apple has now filed its proposal, which reads as follows:

Standard apps (currently subject to the 30% in-app purchase (IAP) commission): 15%; Video Partner Program (VPP), News Partner Program (NPP), Mini Apps Partner Program (MPP), and subscription renewals: 10%; apps under the Small Business Program: 5%.

Apple stated that "factual and expert evidence regarding these proposed commission rates has been submitted concurrently." The company added:

Apple further noted that its "proposed external link commission can also be compared with the commissions charged by other app stores that compete with the App Store," including Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also noted that "the Google Play Store charges a rate of 20% standard, 15% for programs, and 10% for subscriptions on external link transactions—and Epic has agreed to these rates."

Apple stated that the company still believes the fee determination proceedings should be stayed during the Supreme Court's review, and emphasized that filing this proposal is solely to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also pointed out that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket prohibition on charging commissions on external link transactions, and indicated that such commissions are only problematic when they have a de facto prohibitive effect.

With the proposal now filed, Epic will have an opportunity to respond, and Apple expects to submit its arguments to the Supreme Court by September 14.

You can read Apple's full proposal below.
